episodes.title: Episode 07: Four hundred
notes: Goal check (10 fixed games, full game): 391.6, min 341, max 424 (goal ≥ 300); training wrappers: 407.5
Correction: tunnelling does happen (the ball's colour changes by row; the old detector missed it)
Model: GitHub release v1.0; 4 explainer + 4 lesson videos on the site
transcript: Good morning. The run is finished, and the goal is met.

Training ended at half past five, after forty million frames and nine and a half hours on the laptop. Then came the final test, by the rules I wrote down in the middle of the night. Three candidate models each played one hundred fresh games, on seeds nobody had used before. The final model won. It averaged four hundred and eight points, give or take seven. Ninety nine of its hundred games scored three hundred or more. The model from two and a half million frames earlier averaged three hundred and eighty six, and the one before that, three hundred and thirty six. So the last hours of training really did help.

Then the official goal check: the same ten fixed games that every checkpoint played. The final model averaged three hundred and ninety two points. Its worst game scored three hundred and forty one, and its best four hundred and twenty four. The goal was three hundred. With the training wrappers, the same ten games averaged four hundred and eight.

Four hundred is a telling number in Breakout. The first wall is worth four hundred and thirty two points. So the agent clears nearly all of it, almost every game. And it does dig tunnels. One more correction, then: last time I said I saw no tunnels. My detector looked for a red ball, but the ball takes the colour of the row it flies through. With a better test, the twenty and forty million frame models both break through and send the ball above the wall. Most of their points come after that.

What worked. Measuring first. Checking the units of the budget. Writing the test rules down before the answer existed. What I got wrong along the way: the frame budget at the start, a protocol gap that was mostly noise, and the tunnel detector. Each one is written down on the site, with its correction.
Everything is on the site. Four explainer videos about PPO, four lesson videos about how the project works, the replays on the Play tab, and the final model as a download. Thanks for following along.

episodes.title: Episode 06: Over the line, but not yet
notes: 30M frames: 10-game check (fixed seeds 12345-12354, full game) = 332.7 (min 117, max 399)
64 fresh games, same model: 279.7 ± 14.7: the 10-game check was a lucky draw
True level rose from ~170 (20M) to ~280 (30M); games average ~1,780 steps
No tunnelling seen in 3 replayed games at 20M frames
transcript: It is three in the morning, and the run has reached thirty million frames. Three quarters done. I have news that sounds like the finish, and a reason not to celebrate yet.

The news first. The goal check at thirty million frames played the same ten fixed games as every check before it. It averaged three hundred and thirty three points. That is over the goal of three hundred. The worst of the ten games scored one hundred and seventeen, and the best scored three hundred and ninety nine.

Now the reason to wait. Ten games is a small sample. Breakout scores vary by about a hundred points from one game to the next. So I played the same model on sixty four more games, with seeds it had never seen. That average was two hundred and eighty, give or take fifteen. So the model's true level is probably a bit below three hundred, and the ten game check got lucky.

That is exactly why, two hours ago, I wrote down the rules for the final result before it existed. The best candidates get a hundred game test on fresh seeds, and the ten game check is reported next to it. A lucky draw cannot slip through.

The trend is good, though. The true level went from about one hundred and seventy at twenty million frames to about two hundred and eighty now. The games are getting longer too, close to eighteen hundred steps on average. That means the agent is surviving the fast ball in the top rows more often.

And the tunnel? I promised to check. In three replayed games at twenty million frames, the ball never got above the wall. So the high scores so far come from steady brick breaking, not from tunnels. I'll check again with the final model.

What's next. Ten million frames remain, about two and a half hours. The learning rate keeps falling toward zero, so the policy will settle. Around half past five the run ends. Then come the final test, and the last two explainer videos, which need the finished run's numbers.

episodes.title: Episode 05: Halfway, and a correction
notes: 20M frames (50%): goal check 229.7 (full game; min 63, max 384), 185.7 with training wrappers
Correction: the protocol gap (185 vs 139 on 20 games) shrank to 163 vs 146 (SE ~14) on 64 games: mostly noise
A 10-game mean has a standard error of ~35 points; checks now run under both protocols
Run should finish around 06:00
transcript: The run is at twenty million frames, exactly halfway. It is past midnight, and the agent is getting good.

The newest goal check played ten full games on unseen seeds. It averaged about two hundred and thirty points. The best game scored three hundred and eighty four, and the worst sixty three. Two and a half million frames earlier, the check gave about one hundred and eighty. Before that, eighty seven. So the climb I hoped for in the last episode has started.

Now the correction. Last time I worried about a gap. The training games were averaging about one hundred and fifty points, but the goal check gave only eighty seven. I wondered if the way I test was to blame. In training, a lost life ends the episode and the game is soft reset with an automatic fire. In the strict test, nothing happens when a life is lost. The agent has to relaunch the ball itself.

A first test on twenty games seemed to confirm it: one hundred and eighty five against one hundred and thirty nine. But twenty games is not much. So I ran sixty four games each way. The gap shrank to about seventeen points, inside the noise. The real problem was simpler. Breakout scores vary by about a hundred points from game to game. A ten game average is only good to about plus or minus thirty five. The eighty seven was just a low draw. I wrote the mistake down on the site, both the claim and its correction.
Since then, every check runs both ways on the same seeds. At twenty million frames, the strict test happened to score higher than the training-style one. Exactly what noise looks like.

What this means for the goal. The final test is ten games, so the agent needs a true average well above three hundred to pass it reliably. Training games now regularly reach close to four hundred. Twenty million frames remain, about five hours. The run should end around six in the morning. Then I'll check the best models on fresh seeds before claiming anything.

episodes.title: Episode 04: Triple digits
notes: Training mean of 50 games passed 100 at 12.3M frames (expected 14M)
Goal check at 12.5M frames: mean 83.3 (min 41, max 237) on 10 unseen full games
Best training game so far: 304 points (possibly tunnelling; not yet verified on a replay)
About 6.5 hours of training left
transcript: A short update, because something changed fast. At twelve point three million frames, the average of fifty training games passed one hundred points. I had expected that at fourteen million.

The goal check at twelve and a half million frames agrees. Ten full games on unseen seeds averaged eighty three points. That is up from forty nine just two and a half million frames earlier. The spread is wide. The worst game scored forty one, and the best scored two hundred and thirty seven.

That best game is the interesting part. In training, one game already reached three hundred and four points. In Breakout, scores like that often come from tunnelling: the agent breaks through the side of the wall, and the ball bounces around on top, clearing bricks on its own. I haven't watched that game, so I can't say for sure it happened here. I'll check the replays.

Why the sudden speed-up? The bricks at the top are worth more. Yellow ones give four points, and the orange and red ones at the top give seven. So once the agent survives long enough to reach them, the score per minute jumps. The ball also gets faster up there, which is the next thing it must learn to handle.
The training signals still look calm. The typical change per update is small, and about one sample in eight hits the clip.

What's next. The run is just under a third done, with about six and a half hours to go. To reach the goal, the average has to go from eighty three to three hundred. That means tunnelling has to become a habit, not a lucky accident. I'll be back at twenty million frames.

episodes.title: Episode 03: A quarter of the way
notes: 10M frames (25%): training score ~55; goal check mean 48.7 (min 16, max 89) on 10 unseen full games
Approx KL ~0.004-0.006, clip fraction ~12%
Lessons tab: part 1 lessons learned, part 2 narrated lesson videos (setup, screen to input, speed and budgets)
transcript: This is the update at ten million frames. That is a quarter of the run, and it is exactly where the original plan would have stopped.

So what would that plan have delivered? The training games now average about fifty five points. The goal check at ten million frames played ten full games on seeds the agent never trained on. It averaged forty eight point seven points. The worst game scored sixteen, and the best scored eighty nine. With the old plan, the learning rate would be zero now, and this is roughly where the agent would have stayed. Far from three hundred. Stretching the run to forty million frames was the right call.

The goal checks so far tell a clear story. Five points at two and a half million frames. Twelve at five million. Thirty four at seven and a half million. And now forty nine. The score is still climbing steadily, and the checks on unseen games agree with the training numbers.

The training signals look healthy. Each update changes the policy only a little: the measured divergence stays around four to six thousandths. About one sample in eight hits the clip. That is the range the method is meant to work in.

You asked for more depth on how the project works, so the Lessons tab now has two parts. The first part lists the lessons learned. The second part has short narrated videos. One shows how the pieces fit together: the trainer, the evaluator, the website publisher and the studio for videos. One shows how a colour screen becomes the agent's small gray input. And one is about speed, and the units mistake that almost cut the run short. A fourth, on reading PPO's health signals, will use the finished run's curves.

What's next. Thirty million frames remain, about seven and a half hours. Three hundred points means six times today's score, so it is not certain. The jump usually comes once the agent learns to dig a tunnel through the wall. I'll report at twenty million frames, or sooner if the tunnel shows up.

episodes.title: Episode 02: The ball is found
notes: Training score: ~2 until 2M frames, then 4 (2.5M), 9 (3.3M), 14 (4M), ~20 (6M)
First goal check at 2.5M frames: mean 5.4 over 10 unseen full games (min 1, max 9)
Saliency maps on 'How it sees': the actor attends to the ball and paddle
Run at 15% of 40M frames; about 8 hours left
transcript: In the last episode the score was stuck at about two points a game, and I had stretched the run from ten to forty million frames. This is the update two hours later. The short version: learning took off.

For the first two million frames, nothing moved. The average game stayed at two points, about what random button presses get. That flat start is normal for Breakout. The reward comes many steps after the move that earned it, and the agent first has to stumble on the link between the paddle and the ball.

Then, just after two million frames, the curve bent upward. By two and a half million frames the training games averaged about four points. By three and a third million, about nine. By four million, fourteen. Now, at six million frames, it is around twenty points a game. That is ahead of what I wrote down before the run, which was ten points at four million frames.

The first proper goal check was at two and a half million frames. Ten full games, all five lives, on game seeds the agent never trained on. It averaged five point four points, with a worst game of one and a best of nine. So the training numbers and the test numbers agree. That matters, because the training games are counted a little differently.

You can now see what the agent looks at. On the site's How it sees tab, there are saliency maps. They blur a small patch of the input and measure how much the network's answer changes. The actor's map sits right on the ball and on the paddle. The agent found the ball by itself, from gray pixels.
The training itself looks healthy. The policy's randomness is falling slowly, not collapsing. The average change per update stays small, as PPO intends.

What's next. The run is at fifteen percent, and it has about eight hours to go. Three hundred points is still far away. The big jump in Breakout usually comes when the agent learns to dig a tunnel up one side, so the ball bounces around behind the wall. I'll tell you when that happens. Meanwhile, the Lessons tab is getting a second part: short videos that explain how this whole project is set up, from the screen to the published site.

episodes.title: Episode 01: Measure first, and check the units
notes: envpool: ~4,000 agent steps/s vs ~1,800 for gymnasium's AsyncVectorEnv; the full PPO loop ~290 steps/s (4 PyTorch threads)
10-minute smoke test with a mid-way resume: passed, and bit-for-bit reproducible
Correction: CleanRL's 10M = agent steps = 40M frames; run extended from 10M to 40M frames at 1.5M
Video 1 'What PPO does' is on The model tab
transcript: You asked for an agent that learns Breakout from the screen alone, on this laptop, with no graphics card. It has to average three hundred points over ten full games. This is the first update, about one hour in.

I started by measuring. The game simulator, a library called envpool, runs Breakout at about four thousand agent steps a second. The common alternative managed under two thousand. So envpool it is. The whole learning loop is much slower: about two hundred and ninety steps a second. Three quarters of that time goes into the network's update, not into the game. More threads did not help. Eight threads were slower than four, because this laptop has four real cores.

Then a ten minute smoke test. I ran it as two halves, and the second half resumed from the checkpoint the first one left. The resume worked. The second run even reproduced the first one's numbers to the last digit, so the setup is deterministic.

The main run started at eight in the evening. After about one and a half million frames, the score was flat at about two points a game. That is barely better than pressing buttons at random. So I checked the plan against its sources, and found a mistake in the units. The plan said ten million frames, taken from the reference code. But the reference code counts agent steps, and every step is four frames. Its Breakout results are for forty million frames, the same budget as the original paper. With a quarter of that, three hundred points was never likely.

The fix was cheap. I stopped the run at its latest checkpoint and resumed it with forty million frames as the target. The learning rate schedule now stretches over the longer run. Everything is logged: the change is a tag in MLflow and an entry in the site's journal.

What's next. At about three hundred and thirty steps a second, the rest of the run takes around eight hours, so it should finish early tomorrow morning. The first real sign of learning should come around four million frames, when the score ought to climb past ten. If it doesn't, I'll stop and look for a bug before burning the night. Meanwhile I'm making the explainer videos. The first one, on what PPO does, is already on the site.
